rows/rows: A classifier scores an image, x, with one row of weights per class: W times x, one dot product per row. Here, the rows are tree, boat and sunset.
rows/labels: The rows are learned from photos, each with its label: the right answer, written down by a person.
rows/kite: A new class, kite, needs a new row, and that row needs labeled kite photos, and more training.
rows/words: What if the row were written from the class's name instead? Turn the words, a photo of a kite, into a vector, and use it as the row. That is the idea behind CLIP.
space/img: CLIP has two encoders, networks that turn their input into a vector: one reads a photo, the other a caption's tokens, through their embeddings.
space/unit: Both vectors have the same size, and are scaled to length one: every tip lands on one circle, and only the direction counts.
space/sim: Their similarity is the dot product. This photo of a tree and the caption, a tree on a hill, point nearly the same way: zero point nine six. Training must turn every photo toward its own caption, and away from the rest.
train/web: For that, it needs pairs, and the web is full of them: images posted with text beside them. In 2021, Alec Radford and colleagues at OpenAI gathered four hundred million such pairs.
train/batch: Training takes a batch of them at a time: N images and their N captions, each turned into a unit vector of d numbers.
train/sim: One matrix product dots every image with every caption: an N by N grid of similarities.
train/diag: Image i was posted with caption i, so the right pairs lie on the diagonal. For row i, the label, the right answer, is column i.
train/rows: Each row is then a contrastive loss: a softmax over the captions, with a cross-entropy that wants image i to pick caption i. The other N minus one captions in the row are its negatives.
train/cols: Each column gets the same: every caption should pick its own image. The loss averages the two directions.
train/count: With three pairs, the grid holds nine similarities. The three right pairs are pushed up, and the six negatives down, whatever their values now.
train/big: CLIP trained on batches of thirty two thousand, seven hundred and sixty eight pairs, so every row had thirty two thousand, seven hundred and sixty seven negatives.
train/name: Hence the name: contrastive language-image pre-training. Pre-training, because it is trained first, before any one use.
zeroshot/names: Now build a classifier with no labeled photos at all. Write one caption per class: a photo of a tree, a photo of a boat, a photo of a sunset.
zeroshot/prompt: Why a sentence, and not just tree? Radford's team found that web text beside an image is rarely a single word.
zeroshot/embed: Embed the captions and the photo. In two numbers, to fit the circle, the photo points to zero point six, zero point eight.
zeroshot/tree: The tree caption points to zero point eight, zero point six. Their dot product: zero point six times zero point eight, plus zero point eight times zero point six, is zero point nine six.
zeroshot/rest: Boat points to one, zero, and scores zero point six. Sunset points straight down, and scores minus zero point eight. The arg max picks the highest: tree.
zeroshot/W: The caption vectors are the rows of W, with no bias: written from words, not learned from labeled photos.
zeroshot/many: Stack many images as rows, and images times captions transposed gives one row per image, one column per class.
zeroshot/zero: No labeled photo of a tree was used: zero examples, or zero shots. Hence the name, zero-shot classification.
zeroshot/imagenet: On ImageNet, a benchmark of a thousand classes, zero-shot CLIP matched a standard network trained on all one point two eight million of its labeled photos.
